summary: Lecithin is a naturally occurring mixture of phospholipids - predominantly phosphatidylcholine, along with phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylinositol - derived from sources such as soybeans, sunflower, or egg yolk. It is widely used as a food emulsifier and is sold as a dietary supplement marketed as a source of choline and for purported benefits in cholesterol management, liver health, cognition, and (in breastfeeding women) prevention of recurrent blocked milk ducts. It provides choline, a precursor for the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and for cell-membrane phospholipids. There is no FDA-approved therapeutic indication and evidence for most marketed health claims is limited or inconsistent. It is generally well tolerated. NOTE: lecithin is a food substance/dietary supplement, not an FDA-approved drug; this record reflects supplement and food-science references.

moa: Lecithin supplies phospholipids, chiefly phosphatidylcholine. As an amphipathic molecule it acts as an emulsifier, helping to disperse fats in water (the basis of its food and pharmaceutical use). Nutritionally, phosphatidylcholine is a dietary source of choline, which is incorporated into cell-membrane phospholipids, serves as a precursor for the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, and contributes methyl groups (via betaine) to one-carbon metabolism. These roles underlie its use as a nutritional supplement; however, defined pharmacologic therapeutic effects for most marketed claims are not well established.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to lecithin or to its source (e.g., soy or egg allergy, depending on origin)
relative: Soy allergy (for soy-derived lecithin) - choose an alternative source
monitor: Allergic reactions to the source material
Clinical response if used for a specific purpose

preg: Lecithin is generally regarded as safe when consumed at amounts typical of foods and usual supplement doses; it provides choline, which is important during pregnancy. There is limited specific safety data for high-dose supplementation - use sensible amounts and consult a clinician for therapeutic use.
lact: Lecithin is generally considered safe during breastfeeding and is traditionally used (with limited formal evidence) to help prevent recurrent plugged milk ducts; choline supports infant neurodevelopment. Usual food and supplement amounts are not expected to harm the breastfed infant.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment at usual supplement doses. Very high choline intake can theoretically contribute to TMAO production; relevance is uncertain.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is required for hepatic impairment. Phosphatidylcholine has been studied in some liver conditions with inconclusive results; it is not an approved treatment.

major: No clinically significant major drug interactions established
moderate: No clinically significant moderate drug interactions established
minor: Theoretical interaction with anticholinergic drugs (lecithin is a choline source) - not clinically significant at usual doses

interactions.diagnostics: No established laboratory interference at usual intakes.

missed: Lecithin is a dietary supplement without a critical dosing schedule. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered or simply resume the usual schedule; do not take extra to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Lecithin has a wide safety margin. Excessive intake may cause gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort), increased salivation/sweating, and a fishy body odor from high choline. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive, and symptoms resolve on reducing or stopping intake.
